title: An American Haunting
full_review:
"An American Haunting" (After Dark) is an apt title, as it concerns the "Bell Witch" legend, the only documented case in U.S. history of a spirit causing a person's death.

The film uses horror novelist Brent Monahan's "The Bell Witch: An American Haunting" as its foundation, and attempts a revisionist explanation of the mysterious happenings at the home of a Red River, Tenn., family in 1818. The result is a spookily atmospheric, well-acted thriller.

Donald Sutherland is farmer John Bell and Sissy Spacek plays his wife, Lucy. Shortly after John is brought up on charges of usury (a practice against religious law) by the church council, the woman he overcharged in a land dispute -- a crazed harridan thought to be a witch -- curses the family.

Everyone shrugs it off, but before long, their lonely house is beset with things going bump in the night, and John's beloved daughter (Rachel Hurd-Ward) becomes the principal target. The covers are pulled off her in bed, she's dragged across the room, suspended from the ceiling, and repeatedly slapped in the face by the unknown force.

Those outside the family, including schoolmaster Richard Powell (James D'Arcy), are skeptical but soon observe the phenomena themselves. Family friend James Johnston (Matthew Marsh) fails to exorcise the spirit with religious intonations: "Demon, in the name of Jesus Christ, be silent and leave this house forever." (Alas, the spirit most assuredly does not comply.)

In real life, a pre-presidential Andrew Jackson stopped by the Bell household to investigate the strange phenomena.

Writer-director Courtney Solomon builds up a frenzied atmosphere of heady suspense that never lets up. To the film's credit, although there's lots of generalized demonic violence, there's little bloodshed. Horror fans looking for gore may be disappointed, but the otherworldly assaults are quite intense for everyone else, helped immeasurably by the late Adrian Biddle's dizzying photography and Caine Davidson's pulsating score.

Sutherland and Spacek seem quite authentic in their period roles, and Hurd-Ward gives a multifaceted portrayal of the unfortunate object of the poltergeist's attentions, though at the height of her torment she says she doesn't believe in God. At another point, an anguished John rails against God, asking how he could allow this to happen.

The 1818 story is framed by a less interesting contemporary one, involving a divorced woman and her daughter who would seem to have parallels, especially as the daughter is also harassed by demons.

The ending is, unfortunately, somewhat muddled, and (here comes a bit of a spoiler), there would seem to be a sexual component to the scary happenings, but if that is so the explanation is so obtuse that it would certainly go over the heads of most young people, not to mention adults. The version released abroad apparently made this element, coupled with an additional suggestion of a murderous act, much more prominent.

In any case, the U.S. version of "An American Haunting" bears comparison with venerable ghost movies like "The Haunting" and "The Innocents."

The film contains some intensely violent episodes including a hair-raising wolf attack, an attempted suicide, questioning of God's existence and omnipotence, and subtle sexual revelations of an adult nature. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
